LEARNING NOTE / 001

Git

My first steps with version control, alongside my computer science coursework game.

GitCourseworkBeginner

Where I started

I installed Git and learned to use git status and git commit while working on my computer science coursework game. This page brings those first steps together with the supporting commands needed to follow along.

Git records versions of a project. Saving a file updates the copy I am editing; a commit records a chosen set of changes in the project's history. Those are separate actions. That distinction is the starting point for this guide.

The commands and filenames below are teaching examples, rather than a transcript of my coursework. Screenshots from my own project will be added later.

Getting ready

Install Git from the official Git website. On Windows, open Git Bash after installation. Check that Git is available by typing:

git --version

A version number confirms that the terminal can find Git. If the command is not recognised, close and reopen the terminal after installing it.

Before making a first commit, configure the name and email that Git will attach to commits. Replace these example values with the identity you want to use. The --global option sets defaults for your user account.

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Your commit email becomes part of the history and may be visible if you publish the repository, so choose an address you are comfortable including.

Start in the project folder

Open a terminal in the folder containing your game project. In Git Bash, you can move to a folder with cd. The path here is an example; use your own folder's location.

cd "/c/Users/YourName/Documents/coursework-game"
git status

If this is already a Git repository, the status command will describe its current state. If Git says it is not a repository, and this is the project folder you want to track, initialise it:

git init

This creates a hidden .git directory where Git stores the repository's history and settings. You do not need a GitHub account to keep local commits.

Before adding files, create an appropriate .gitignore for your game engine or tools. Generated build folders, caches and private credentials generally do not belong in the repository. The exact ignore rules depend on your project.

Check what has changed

git status

This command reports the current branch and the state of your files. It does not change them. It helps answer a useful question before committing: what is Git about to record?

Untracked files
Files Git has not started tracking yet.
Changes not staged for commit
Changes in tracked files that have not been selected for the next commit.
Changes to be committed
The staged changes selected for the next commit.

Choose what goes into the commit

Git has a staging area: the selection of changes you want in the next commit. To select a file, use git add with its actual path. For example, a game might have a file called player.py:

git add player.py
git status

Replace player.py with a file that exists in your project. The second command lets you check that it now appears under changes to be committed.

Staging captures the file's content at that moment. If you edit it again before committing, run git add again to include those later edits. You can inspect the staged changes with:

git diff --staged

Choosing specific files is helpful while learning because it makes the selection explicit. You do not need to include every changed file in a single commit.

Record a commit

Once the right changes are staged, record them with a message explaining the change:

git commit -m "Describe the change you made"

The -m option supplies the message directly in the command. For a game, a message might describe a movement adjustment or a menu fix—but it should describe what you actually changed.

A normal commit records the staged changes, rather than automatically including every edit in the folder. If Git reports that there is nothing to commit, use git status to check whether changes still need staging.

git status
git log --oneline

Status checks what remains after the commit. The log shows a short history of commits. A clean working tree means there are no outstanding changes Git is reporting; ignored files can still exist.

A commit is stored locally. It does not upload your project or create an off-device backup. Sharing with a remote repository is a separate step.

A small routine to build on

After making and saving a meaningful change in your editor, check the changes, stage the relevant files, review them, and commit:

git status
git add your-file.ext
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Describe the change"
git status

Replace the example filename and message each time. Smaller commits that explain one useful change make the history easier to read than a single commit containing unrelated work.

This is a starting workflow. My experience described here is installing Git and using status and commit for my coursework game; this article does not claim experience with team workflows, branching or merging.
